nodes.label: Minimal IAM policy for S3 storage
nodes.rationale: The policy grants only s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and prefix-scoped s3:ListBucket. s3:DeleteObject is deliberately omitted because MFE Orchestrator never deletes artifacts, so a compromised key cannot destroy release history; housekeeping should use lifecycle rules which need no credentials.
nodes.norm_label: minimal iam policy for s3 storage

nodes.label: Azure Blob Storage integration
nodes.rationale: Three authentication methods are offered: connection string (quick but account-wide), shared key (container-scoped but derived from an account key), and Azure AD service principal (recommended for production).

nodes.label: Azure AD service principal authentication
nodes.rationale: Recommended for production. Storage Blob Data Contributor scoped at the container is the least-privilege choice: Reader is insufficient (uploads fail) and Owner grants more than needed. Client secrets expire, which is the most common cause of a storage that worked for months and then failed.

nodes.label: Google Cloud Storage integration
nodes.rationale: Storage Object Admin granted on the single bucket is the right scope: objectViewer is insufficient for uploads and storage.admin grants bucket administration the platform does not need.

nodes.label: Service account JSON key
nodes.rationale: The entire JSON document must be pasted because the platform reads client_email and private_key out of it. Keys do not expire by default, which is convenient but a long-term risk, so rotation on a schedule is advised.

nodes.label: Storage (Bucket)
nodes.rationale: Using your own bucket gives data residency control and your own retention/backup policy, which is the right answer for production and compliance; the hub is for getting started and self-hosted installs. The provider type is fixed at creation.

nodes.label: Server-side streaming from private buckets
nodes.rationale: MFE Orchestrator reads objects server-side with the configured credentials and streams them to browsers itself, so the bucket never needs to be public and never needs CORS configuration - the browser talks to the platform, not to the bucket.

nodes.label: Deterministic storage path layout
nodes.rationale: Files land at <path>/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<microfrontendSlug>/<version>/. The project id in the prefix lets several projects and installations share one bucket without colliding; versions sit side by side and nothing is deleted or overwritten, which is what makes rollback instant.

nodes.label: API Key
nodes.rationale: Authenticates a machine against a single project, sent in the api-key header (query parameter discouraged because it leaks into logs). Shown once and stored hashed. One key per consumer keeps the blast radius correct; a leaked MANAGER key can publish arbitrary JavaScript to production.

nodes.label: Mandatory API key expiry
nodes.rationale: There is no non-expiring key by design: a credential that never expires is one nobody ever rotates. The trade-off is that an expired key fails pipelines at upload time, after a successful build, which is confusing if the expiry was forgotten.

nodes.label: Generated Azure Pipelines pipeline
nodes.rationale: Deliberately split into Build and Deploy stages: Build runs on branch pushes and tags so every commit gets CI feedback, while Deploy runs only on tags, so a tag publishes and the version is derived by stripping refs/tags/ from the tag name.

nodes.label: mfe-orchestrator-upload Azure DevOps task
nodes.rationale: An Azure DevOps extension that must be installed in the organization; if third-party extensions are not permitted, it can be replaced by a curl call to the upload endpoint, which does the same thing.

nodes.label: MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS variable group
nodes.rationale: Created at project scope so several microfrontend repositories in the same Azure DevOps project share it; holds the MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY variable and may need first-run pipeline authorization.

nodes.label: Generated GitHub Actions build-and-deploy workflow
nodes.rationale: Triggers only on tags and manual dispatch - a push to main does nothing by design. Tag-driven versioning is what makes the console's Build button work. For production the deployment step is left manual because the separation between published and live is the platform's main safety property.

nodes.label: mfe-orchestrator-hub/github-action publish action
nodes.rationale: Zips the file-path directory and calls the upload endpoint; it should be pointed at the directory, not at a pre-made zip.

nodes.label: Generated GitLab CI pipeline
nodes.rationale: Unlike the GitHub and Azure DevOps templates, the scaffolded GitLab pipeline stops at build - it produces dist/ as an artifact but does not publish, so the deploy job must be added by hand.

nodes.label: GitLab CI deploy job
nodes.rationale: only: tags keeps publishing tied to tags (which powers the console Build action) and CI_COMMIT_TAG supplies the version; curl --fail is essential or the job passes even when the upload is rejected; the zip is created from inside dist so the archive has no directory prefix.

nodes.label: Upload endpoint (POST /microfrontends/by-slug/{slug}/upload/{version})
nodes.rationale: Everything the provider-specific pipelines do reduces to this one HTTP call: multipart ZIP upload authenticated by api-key header, project derived from the key. Re-uploading an existing version overwrites in place, which silently changes what deployed users get, so publishing a new version is preferred. Custom URL microfrontends cannot be uploaded to.

nodes.label: ZIP archive layout rule
nodes.rationale: The archive must contain the contents of the build output, not the folder itself; a dist/ prefix inside the zip shifts the entry point to dist/assets/remoteEntry.js, mismatching the configured entry point so every request 404s. Zip from inside the output directory.

nodes.label: Project
nodes.rationale: The top-level container and the boundary for authorization: every other object belongs to exactly one project and access is granted per project. Selected in direct API calls via the project-id header.

nodes.label: Environment
nodes.rationale: A deployment stage inside a project (dev, uat, prod). Its domains list lets public endpoints resolve which environment a browser request belongs to from the Referer header, so a single microfrontend URL serves the right version per stage.

nodes.label: Microfrontend (host or remote)
nodes.rationale: A versioned frontend bundle, either a host (shell) or a remote. Parent/child relations declared in the console are turned into the remotes block of the Module Federation configuration.

nodes.label: Environment variable (global variable)
nodes.rationale: A key/value pair scoped to one environment, read at runtime by the browser rather than baked in at build time, so the same artifact can be promoted from uat to prod without a rebuild.

nodes.label: Deployment (immutable snapshot)
nodes.rationale: The single most important idea in MFE Orchestrator: editing is not deploying. Changes sit in the project configuration until Deploy freezes them into a numbered immutable snapshot and activates it; exactly one is active per environment, and rollback is re-activating an older one.

nodes.label: Lifecycle of a change (commit to browser)
nodes.rationale: Commit, build and upload via CI, version registration, deployment, then serving: the host asks the public serve API which URLs to load and the active deployment answers.
nodes.norm_label: lifecycle of a change (commit to browser)

nodes.label: Deployment snapshot
nodes.rationale: Captures every microfrontend (version, hosting, entry point, canary settings, relations), every environment variable and every storage configuration as a copy, not references - editing afterwards does not reach back into it. This is why production can serve 1.2.0 while 1.4.0 is staged for UAT.

nodes.label: Promotion between environments
nodes.rationale: There is no dedicated promote button because promotion is just a deployment: select the version live in the source environment and deploy the target. The artifact is not rebuilt or copied - what differs between stages is only the environment variables each snapshot carries.

nodes.label: Rollback
nodes.rationale: Because deployments are immutable snapshots, rollback is re-activating an existing snapshot - no rebuild, revert commit or re-upload. It restores versions, hosting, canary settings and variables together, which matters when an incident has more than one cause. It does not restore the draft configuration, so the selected version must be reconciled afterwards or the next deployment re-ships the bad version.

nodes.label: Redeploy
nodes.rationale: Redeploy re-activates the same snapshot with a fresh timestamp and does not pick up draft changes; Deploy takes a new snapshot. Deployment numbers are never reused, so #7 active after #9 tells you at a glance a rollback happened.

nodes.label: Allowed Domains
nodes.rationale: Building the environment into the URL makes the host artifact environment-specific, the very thing microfrontend architectures should avoid. Registering the domains each environment is served from lets one artifact serve every stage. Each domain must be registered on exactly one environment or resolution is ambiguous.

nodes.label: Referer-based environment resolution
nodes.rationale: Environment-less endpoints (auto, mfeId-only forms) read the browser's Referer header and match it against registered domains to find the environment, then answer from that environment's active deployment. Endpoints naming the environment explicitly ignore the domain list. Matching is case-insensitive on the Referer and its origin.

nodes.label: Runtime environment variables
nodes.rationale: Build-time variables make the artifact environment-specific, so promoting means rebuilding and the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped. Runtime variables let one artifact travel through every stage with the stage supplying configuration. Captured in the deployment snapshot, so a config change is as auditable and reversible as a code change.

nodes.label: Environment variables are not a secret store
nodes.rationale: Variables are served to the browser by a public, unauthenticated endpoint; anyone with the project and environment id can read them. Use them only for public configuration - API base URLs, feature flags, tracking ids, public keys - never secrets.
nodes.norm_label: environment variables are not a secret store

nodes.label: Environments as deployment stages
nodes.rationale: Microfrontends, storages, repositories, API keys and members are project-scoped; variables and deployments are environment-scoped. A microfrontend exists once but the live version is a property of each environment's active deployment - the mechanism by which one definition serves many stages. Environment slugs are public and renaming breaks serve URLs.

nodes.label: Module Federation with Vite
nodes.rationale: target: 'esnext' is required because Module Federation relies on top-level await; minify: false and cssCodeSplit: false avoid known chunk-rewriting issues in the plugin. Vite builds emit assets/remoteEntry.js, so the Entry Point must be set accordingly. Generated remote URLs contain no version or environment - both resolve server-side from the active deployment.

nodes.label: @originjs/vite-plugin-federation
nodes.rationale: The Module Federation implementation for Vite; it only emits remoteEntry.js on vite build, so vite dev cannot serve federated remotes - develop against a built preview or the deployed remote.

nodes.label: Module Federation with Webpack
nodes.rationale: Webpack remote syntax is name@url, not the bare URL Vite uses. Webpack writes remoteEntry.js at the output root so the default Entry Point stays remoteEntry.js. The generated config marks shared deps eager: true, trading a larger initial bundle for a simpler startup with no async boundary; production hosts with a bundle budget should drop eager and use the import('./bootstrap') pattern.

nodes.label: ModuleFederationPlugin (Webpack 5)
nodes.rationale: Built into Webpack 5, no extra dependency. requiredVersion with singleton: true makes Webpack warn at runtime on shared-library major-version mismatches - the source of most confusing microfrontend bugs.

nodes.label: Integration page
nodes.rationale: Generates, per selected environment and host, the exact snippets a project needs with ids pre-filled; requires an active deployment because there is nothing to integrate against until then. Inject in Repository writes the generated configuration directly into a connected repository.

nodes.label: Build-time configuration model
nodes.rationale: Copy the generated remotes block into the bundler config: simplest, standard Module Federation. URLs contain no version numbers so version bumps are still just deployments, but adding or removing a remote requires a host rebuild. The recommended starting point.

nodes.label: Runtime discovery model
nodes.rationale: The host asks the serve API at boot which remotes exist and registers them dynamically: adding a remote needs no host rebuild, at the cost of dynamic remote loading code and one HTTP request at startup. Teams move to it when the roster of remotes changes often.

nodes.label: window.globalConfig runtime configuration script
nodes.rationale: A blocking script in <head> assigns window.globalConfig before the bundle runs, so configuration is guaranteed to exist - no loading state, no race - which is why it is the default recommendation over fetching JSON, which adds an asynchronous startup dependency. All values are strings, so compare explicitly ('true'). The variables endpoints do not resolve environment from the request domain, so an id or slug is always required.

nodes.label: Serve API
nodes.rationale: Public and unauthenticated by design - called from browsers, where a credential could not be kept secret anyway; the management API is a separate authenticated surface. Every endpoint answers from the active deployment of the resolved environment. Endpoints come in id, projectId+slug, and Referer-resolved flavours.

nodes.label: /serve/all endpoint
nodes.rationale: Returns the whole environment in one call - microfrontends with resolved URLs and versions plus variables. nameToIntegrate is the Module Federation remote name (slug with / and - stripped). The endpoint to build runtime discovery on.

nodes.label: Entry point no-cache headers
nodes.rationale: The microfrontend entry point is served with Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate while every other file is cacheable. The uncacheable entry point is what makes a deployment take effect promptly: browsers re-fetch it, discover the new hashed chunk names, and load those from cache or network.

nodes.label: MFE Orchestrator Online Console
nodes.rationale: Hosted console recommended for the tutorial because it requires no setup and is always up to date, versus self-hosting which gives full control and custom configuration.

nodes.label: Canary Release
nodes.rationale: Serves a new version to a fraction of traffic per microfrontend without any host application change; the host receives one URL per remote and does not know which side of the split it got, so no client-side logic is required. Feature is experimental: session-based distribution works, but user-based and cookie-based targeting are incomplete and the Canary Users page is marked Coming soon.

nodes.label: Canary Deployment Type (Based on Version / Based on URL)
nodes.rationale: Based on version is the natural choice when the canary is the next build; based on URL is useful when the candidate lives on separate infrastructure (preview environment, different CDN) and you want to route a traffic slice there without registering it as a version.
nodes.norm_label: canary deployment type (based on version / based on url)

nodes.label: Environment-based Progressive Rollout (Canary Alternative)
nodes.rationale: Until canary support stabilises, the most reliable progressive rollout is to mirror production in an environment, route a traffic subset via your own routing/DNS, deploy the candidate there and promote by deploying the same version to production — it uses only the fully implemented deployment mechanics and keeps rollback a single redeploy away.

nodes.label: Create From Template
nodes.rationale: Fastest path from nothing to a deployable microfrontend: creates the repository, pushes the template as initial commit, injects a provider-specific build pipeline pre-filled with slug and API base URL, and creates an API key stored as a provider secret — so the generated pipeline works on its first run with no key copied by hand.

nodes.label: Create From Scratch
nodes.rationale: For code that already exists: same general information plus hosting configuration (Hub, Custom Source, Custom URL). MFE Orchestrator will not add a pipeline to a repository it did not create — copy one from template-pipelines and create an API key yourself.

nodes.label: MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY Secret
nodes.rationale: API key with the MANAGER role, valid one year, stored in the Git provider as secret MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY (on Azure DevOps inside the MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS variable group); it is the credential the generated pipeline uses to upload build artifacts.

nodes.label: Hosts and Remotes in Module Federation (Doc)
nodes.norm_label: hosts and remotes in module federation (doc)

nodes.label: Microfrontend Relation Graph (Parents/Hosts)
nodes.rationale: The graph is what lets the platform generate Module Federation configuration: a host's remotes are computed as all microfrontends in the active deployment whose parents include that host, each resolved to a concrete URL from its hosting type and frozen version. Consequence: the host's build config contains remote names only — bumping a remote version in production is a deployment, not a host rebuild. A remote can be a host of other remotes and can have several parents.

nodes.label: Remote Name Derivation from Slug
nodes.rationale: Module Federation remote names cannot contain '/' or '-', so the name is derived from the slug by stripping them (product-catalog -> productcatalog, shop/catalog -> shop_catalog). Prefer dash-free slugs so imports stay readable and unambiguous.

nodes.label: Shared Singleton Dependencies
nodes.rationale: Generated configs mark react, react-dom and react-router-dom as shared singletons to prevent two copies of React loading — a failure mode that produces confusing hook errors rather than an obvious crash. Other shared libraries must be added to the shared block of every participating microfrontend, hosts and remotes alike.

nodes.label: Hosting Type
nodes.rationale: Every microfrontend declares where its files live; the hosting type determines how a request for remoteEntry.js is resolved into actual bytes.

nodes.label: MFE Orchestrator Hub Hosting
nodes.rationale: Platform stores the build itself; files land on the server filesystem under MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<microfrontendSlug>/<version>/. When self-hosting, mount MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER on a persistent volume (upload_microfrontends in the reference docker-compose.yaml) or every container restart loses uploaded builds. Best for getting started, internal tools, self-hosted installations.

nodes.label: Custom Source (Own Bucket) Hosting
nodes.rationale: Build stored in a bucket you own (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) and streamed on request; the bucket does not need to be public because files are fetched server-side with configured credentials and streamed through the serve API. Best for production, compliance, keeping artifacts inside your cloud account. Only appears as an option once the project has at least one storage configured.

nodes.label: Custom URL Hosting
nodes.rationale: Files already published elsewhere (CDN, static host); MFE Orchestrator only tracks versions and hands the right URL to the host. Upload is rejected. URL placeholders ($version, $microfrontendSlug, $projectId, $projectSlug) are substituted at request time — $version makes switching a version in the console and deploying enough to repoint users at different CDN files with no host rebuild.

nodes.label: Entry Point
nodes.rationale: Names the file consumers load; defaults to index.js but Module Federation builds usually produce remoteEntry.js (Webpack) or assets/remoteEntry.js (Vite). Always served with Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate while surrounding hashed assets stay cacheable — that is what lets a deployment take effect immediately without stale chunks. All served files carry Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin so hosts on other origins can load them.

nodes.label: Host Microfrontend (Shell)
nodes.rationale: The shell application: boots the page, owns routing and layout, and loads remotes at runtime. A project normally has one host per application.

nodes.label: Remote Microfrontend
nodes.rationale: A microfrontend exposed to be consumed by a host. A remote can itself be a host of other remotes — relations form a graph, not just a two-level tree.

nodes.label: Microfrontend Slug
nodes.rationale: Lowercase, URL-friendly, unique within the project, fixed at creation: the slug appears in serve URLs and becomes the Module Federation remote name, so the console makes the field read-only when editing — changing it means creating a new microfrontend and re-pointing consumers.

nodes.label: Microfrontend Version
nodes.rationale: A version is an opaque string you choose: MFE Orchestrator does not parse or order versions, it uses them as folder names and as the value handed to the host application. What users actually load is the version captured in the active deployment, not the one selected in the form.

nodes.label: Console Build Action (Tag Creation)
nodes.source_location: Triggering a build from the console
nodes.rationale: Pressing Start Build does one thing: it creates a Git tag named after the version on the head of the selected branch. Everything else happens in CI — the generated pipelines are tag-triggered, which is why it works out of the box; a custom pipeline must trigger on tags or the Build button creates tags nothing acts on. Requires a linked code repository.

nodes.label: Continuous Deployment Flag
nodes.rationale: A marker, not an automation: published to consumers as continuousDeployment on the serve API payload, but the platform does not change version resolution based on it. It is metadata your own tooling can act on (e.g. a host polling for updates on CD remotes). To reach an environment without a manual step, call POST <API_BASE>/deployment from the pipeline after upload.

nodes.label: Project (Top-level Container)
nodes.rationale: The top-level container and access-control boundary: microfrontends, environments, storages, code repositories, API keys and members belong to exactly one project. Rule of thumb: one project per application, because microfrontends can only be wired into a host graph within a project and API keys are project-scoped — splitting an application across projects loses the relation graph that generates Module Federation config. Deleting a project is irreversible and immediately breaks every public serve endpoint; files in your own buckets, template-created Git repos and provider secrets survive.

nodes.label: project-id API Header
nodes.rationale: Management API calls select the project with a project-id header (some endpoints also take environment-id); requests authenticated with an API key derive the project from the key and do not need the header.

nodes.label: Project Roles (Admin/Editor/Viewer = OWNER/MEMBER/VIEWER)
nodes.rationale: Access granted per project; console labels (Admin/Editor/Viewer) differ from API/database names (OWNER/MEMBER/VIEWER). There is no per-environment permission split: an Editor who can deploy dev can deploy prod — restrict production either via a separate project or by limiting Editor membership. Keep Admins few but never one. Machine access should use API keys (MANAGER/VIEWER roles, expiring, revocable), not shared service users; keys belong to the project, so audit them when a person leaves.

nodes.label: Azure DevOps Personal Access Token
nodes.source_location: Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)
nodes.rationale: Requires exact scopes: Code, Build and Release at Read, write & manage, plus Variable Groups at Read, create & manage — the last one lets MFE Orchestrator create the MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS variable group where the pipeline's API key is stored.

nodes.label: GitHub OAuth Authorization
nodes.rationale: Unlike GitLab and Azure DevOps, GitHub does not ask for a Personal Access Token: you authorize MFE Orchestrator via OAuth and it holds the credential. Scopes requested: repo, public_repo, read:user, read:org, workflow, admin:org. Organization repositories require granting org access, and some organizations require an owner to approve third-party OAuth apps before repos appear.

nodes.label: GitLab Personal Access Token
nodes.source_location: Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)
nodes.rationale: Requires scopes api, read_user and read_repository; writes (pushing a template into a new repository, committing generated configuration) go through the API, which the api scope already covers. Works for GitLab.com and self-hosted instances (GitLab 8.8+).

nodes.label: Docker Compose Stack (MongoDB + Redis + MFE Orchestrator)
nodes.rationale: Reference docker-compose.yaml runs mongo:latest, redis:alpine and lory1990/mfe-orchestrator:latest together, wiring NOSQL_DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL and MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER, with persistent volumes mongodb_data, redis_data and upload_microfrontends.
nodes.norm_label: docker compose stack (mongodb + redis + mfe orchestrator)

nodes.norm_label: use an external mongodb and redis (doc)

nodes.label: External MongoDB and Redis for Production
nodes.rationale: For production, external managed database and cache services (MongoDB Atlas, AWS DocumentDB, Redis Cloud, ElastiCache, Memorystore) are strongly recommended over embedded instances: higher reliability, better performance, easier maintenance, horizontal scalability, and simplified backup and recovery. Configured via NOSQL_DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL/REDIS_PASSWORD.
nodes.norm_label: external mongodb and redis for production

nodes.label: Microfrontend Template
nodes.rationale: A working Module Federation project — correct build configuration, a sample exposed component and a matching CI pipeline — so a new microfrontend is deployable in minutes. The valuable part is the federation config plus the build settings MF requires (target: esnext, minify: false, cssCodeSplit: false), which are easy to get wrong by hand and produce obscure runtime failures. Templates come in host/remote pairs; picking the wrong one is the most common early mistake.

nodes.label: marketplace.json Template Manifest
nodes.rationale: The catalogue is assembled from marketplace/marketplace.json in the documentation repository, fetched at request time — so new templates appear in every installation, hosted and self-hosted, without an upgrade. Each entry declares name, framework, compiler, host type, entry point, repository and download URL; type and compiler double as the lookup key <type>/<compiler>/<provider> selecting which pipeline is injected. comingSoon: true shows a badged, unselectable entry.

nodes.label: template-pipelines Repository
nodes.rationale: Holds the provider-specific build-and-deploy pipelines injected at scaffold time, organised by <type>/<compiler>/<provider>. A template whose combination has no pipeline is still usable but no CI file is added. Also the place to copy pipelines from when bringing your own repository.
